newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia financiers say recession is supply-driven.
newsitem.headline: Colombia financiers say recession is supply-driven.

text.p: Private sector fears over low returns on investments are fueling Colombia's recession, not a short-term fall in consumer demand, an influential financial group said Sunday.

In his weekly report, Armando Montenegro, head of the National Association of Financial Institutions (ANIF) said the strong peso currency, high wage costs, tax increases and unfair competition from contraband goods had created an uncertain business climate in the country.

Last week, the government's National Planning Department said Colombia's gross domestic product (GDP) fell by 1.22 percent in the first quarter this year, following a 0.1 percent drop in the fourth quarter of 1996. The news meant that Colombia was officially in recession for the first time in more than 50 years.

"This recession was not caused by (soft) demand, nor is it short-term," Montenegro said in his report. "It is above all a recession caused by low supply because of a series of obstacles placed in the way of production, job creation and capital formation."

Last Friday, the National Statistics Department reported industrial output, excluding coffee processing, in February was 7.39 percent down compared with the same month last year -- the worst fall in 15 years.

"Economic policy in the last few years has not favored private enterprise," Montenegro said. "Returns on investment have fallen and profit margins are falling because of the revaluation of the peso, high real wages and hikes in taxes."
Last year, the peso gained 14 percent in real terms. But the national minimum wage, which serves as a benchmark for wage hikes throughout the private sector, fell in real terms.
The increase announced by President Ernesto Samper's government in January was 21.02 percent -- below 1996 inflation of 21.63 percent.

Montenegro repeated concerns already voiced by many Colombian businessmen and the International Monetary Fund that Samper's economic policy is focused on short-term solutions instead of resolving Colombia's underlying structural problems.

He called for the government to tackle the burgeoning fiscal deficit, to limit the transfer of funds from central government to local government, to change the social security regime and to accelerate plans to sell off state-owned industries.
